subject: chemistry
question_text: Calculate the molarity of NaOH in the solution prepared by dissolving 4 g in enough water to form 250 mL of the solution.

verification.note: Chapter 5 (Stoichiometry) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.66-72), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Formula and substitution

lines.text: Molarity M = (weight / GMW) × (1000 / V in mL)

steps.why: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. Weight over GMW gives the moles, and 1000 over the volume in mL scales the given volume up to one litre.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the 1000/V factor and answering 0.1 M.
Using the mass of water instead of the volume of the SOLUTION. Molarity is per litre of solution.
steps.memory_tip: Molarity is per litre of soLution. Molality (later) is per kilogram of solvent.
steps.margin_note: The formula with GMW = 40 substituted earns this mark.

steps.label: The answer with its unit
steps.why: 4/40 = 0.1 mol of NaOH sits in 250 mL; one litre is four times 250 mL, so one litre would hold 0.4 mol.
common_mistakes: Writing 0.4 with no unit. The unit M (mol L⁻¹) is part of the mark.
steps.memory_tip: A quarter litre holds 0.1 mol, so a full litre holds 4 times that: 0.4 mol.
steps.margin_note: Box 0.4 M. Writing mol L⁻¹ beside it is equally accepted.

insider_note: The 1000/V factor is the whole trap: 0.1 M (moles alone) is the standard wrong answer, and the examiner looks for the volume scaling written out.
